statements.claim: In the dead of night Shambara, the shape-shifting asura, stole the newborn son of Rukmini from the lying-in chamber of Dvaraka, unseen by nurse or guard.
statements.evidence: BP 10.55.2: 'taṃ śambaraḥ kāma-rūpī hṛtvā tokam anirdaśam'; Harivamsha 1.251: 'On the seventh day at dead of night Kalashamvara stole away that infant son of Krishna from the lying-in room'; VP 5.27: 'stolen from the lying-in chamber by Sambara, terrible as death'.

statements.claim: The child had been in the world not yet ten days when he was taken.
statements.evidence: BP 10.55.2 'anirdaśam' (not ten days old); variant ages (six days per VP, seventh night per Harivamsha) are consistent with 'not yet ten days'.

statements.claim: The infant was Pradyumna, born to Rukmini of Krishna's potency, and was Kama reborn — Kama of firm vows, who had been reduced to ashes, took this birth from Rukmini (Lakshmi in human form) and Krishna in order to kill Shambara.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.251: 'Kāma (Cupid) of firm vows, in order to kill Shamvara, took his birth from Rukshmini, the incarnation of Lakshmi, and Vāsudeva as his beautiful son Pradyumna'; also 'He was formerly reduced to ashes by the divine trident handed deity'; BP pack excerpt (10.55.1): 'Pradyumna was born to Rukmini of Krishna's potency'.

statements.claim: Shambara carried the foreknowledge that this child, if he lived, would be his destroyer.
statements.evidence: VP 5.27: 'for the demon foreknew that Pradyumna, if he lived, would be his destroyer'.

statements.claim: Shambara carried the child to the ocean and cast him into the sea — deep waters swarming with monsters, where whirlpools roar and huge creatures of the deep make their haunts.
statements.evidence: VP 5.27: 'Sambara cast him into the ocean, swarming with monsters, into a whirlpool of roaring waves, the haunt of the huge creatures of the deep'; BP rendered pack excerpt (10.55.1-2): 'stole the newborn and threw him into the ocean'.

statements.claim: Krishna, wrapped in his own divine Maya, knew everything — the thief and where the child was going — and yet did not strike the demon down as he crept through the palace.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.251: 'Krishna, who followed the celestial Māyā, knew every thing and therefore he did not kill at that time the Dānava, invincible in battle. As if urged on by Death the great Asura stole away Krishna's son.'

statements.claim: Rukmini mourned her lost son like a cow mourning the calf taken from her, while the palace women wept and the search at dawn found nothing.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.251 (in pack): 'your mother is bewailing like a cow estranged from its calf.' The dawn-search and weeping-women scenes are connective elaboration consistent with that grief.

statements.claim: Far below the waves a great fish was already moving through the deep toward the place where the child had fallen.
statements.evidence: BP 10.55.3 (pack forward-link, next story DKS_0336): 'taṃ nirjagāra balavān mīnaḥ' (a mighty fish swallowed him); closing image phrased as atmosphere.

notes: Internal pack inconsistency, not flagged: the Harivamsha (Dutt) passage in this pack says Shambara carried the child to his own city and gave him to Mayavati, while the pack's variant_notes say all three sources cast him into the sea. The story follows the BP/VP sea-casting rendering (primary source, confidence 5), affirmed by the index summary and variant note as the intended reading.

statements.claim: A mighty fish swallowed the infant whole as the ocean closed over him; the fish was later caught by fishermen, who presented it as a gift to the demon Shambara.
statements.evidence: BP 10.55.3-4: 'taṃ nirjagāra balavān mīnaḥ... taṃ śambarāya kaivartā upājahrur upāyanam'.

statements.claim: In Shambara's palace the fish went to the kitchens, where his wife Mayavati oversaw the cooks; when the great fish was cut open, a living, unharmed child was found curled in its belly and brought to Mayavati.
statements.evidence: BP 10.55.5 & 7: 'dṛṣṭvā tad-udare bālam māyāvatyai nyavedayan'; 'nirūpitā śambareṇa sā sūdaudana-sādhane'; VP 5.27: Mayavati 'superintended the operations of the cooks, and saw, when the fish was cut open, a beautiful child'.

statements.claim: Mayavati was not simply the demon's wife: she was Rati, wife of Kama, the god of love long since reduced to ashes.
statements.evidence: BP 10.55.6: 'sā ca kāmasya vai patnī ratir nāma yaśasvinī'; Kama's reduction to ashes per Harivamsha 1.251 (sibling pack): 'He was formerly reduced to ashes by the divine trident handed deity'.

statements.claim: Mayavati recognized the child at once as her husband reborn — the son of Vasudeva and Rukmini, stolen from Dvaraka and thrown into the sea — and took him as her own, telling no one who he was.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.251: 'Seeing him she was filled with joy... she recollected that he was her favourite husband... he has been seen by me in another birth'; pack rendered excerpt (BP 10.55.3-14): 'who — being Rati, Kama's wife — knew him and raised him, later revealing he was Krishna's son'. The 'told no one' secrecy accords with the boy knowing Mayavati only as his mother.

statements.claim: The child grew up in Shambara's palace believing Mayavati was his mother and the demon his father; she nursed and reared him and taught him the arts of illusion, and in a short time he passed into full youth — lotus-eyed, long-armed, the fairest sight in the world of men.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.251: Pradyumna 'out of ignorance knew Māyāvati as his mother... Māyāvati too... instructed him in all forms of illusion'; BP 10.55.8-9: 'nāti-dīrgheṇa kālena sa kārṣṇi rūḍha-yauvanaḥ... padma-dalāyatekṣaṇaṃ pralamba-bāhuṃ nara-loka-sundaram'; pack variant note cross-refs the Harivamsha expansion (hv_b2_042-047).

statements.claim: When Mayavati came to the grown youth as a woman comes to a man, he stepped back in astonishment and protested: 'Mother, your mind is set otherwise.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.55.10: 'tām aha bhagavān kārṣṇir mātas te matir anyathā'.

statements.claim: Mayavati then told him the truth — he was not her son nor Shambara's, but the son of Vasudeva and Rukmini of the Vrishni line; Shambara had thrown him into the sea before he was ten days old; he must kill that enemy of his life; and his mother in Dvaraka still mourned him like a female osprey bereft of her young.
statements.evidence: BP 10.55.12-14: 'eṣa tvānirdaśaṃ sindhāv akṣipac chambaro 'suraḥ / tam imaṃ jahi durdharṣaṃ durjayaṃ śatrum ātmanaḥ / parīśocati te mātā kurarīva gata-prajā'. The gloss 'unconquerable only while he is unknown' is interpretive coloring of durdharṣa/durjaya, not a separate sourceable fact.

notes: Story follows the Bhagavata version (fish/cook/recognition), which the pack's primary source and its own tradition_note affirm; the Harivamsha 'awake and told by Narada' variant is acknowledged in the story's tradition_note, matching the pack.

statements.claim: When Mayavati had told Pradyumna who he truly was, she gave him the Maha-vidya — the great science that destroys all illusion, the one art that could stand against the demon's sorcery.
statements.evidence: BP 10.55.15: 'prabhāṣyaivaṃ dadau vidyāṃ pradyumnāya mahātmane'; pack rendered excerpt: 'Mayavati gave Pradyumna the Maha-vidya that destroys all illusion'.

statements.claim: Armed with it, Pradyumna approached Shambara and called him out to battle — in the open and alone, not by stealth as the demon had once come to Dvaraka.
statements.evidence: BP 10.55.16: 'sa ca śambaram abhyetya saṃyugāya samāhvayat'. 'Alone / in the open' is connective emphasis consistent with an open challenge.

statements.claim: Stung by the young man's harsh words as a serpent is stung by a foot, Shambara seized his great mace, whirled it over his head and hurled it; Pradyumna struck the flying mace down in mid-air with a mace of his own.
statements.evidence: BP 10.55.17-19: 'so 'dhikṣipto durvācobhiḥ padāhata ivoragaḥ / gadām āvidhya tarasā pradyumnāya mahātmane / tām āpatantīṃ bhagavān pradyumno gadayā gadām'.

statements.claim: Shambara then resorted to the Daitya illusion that the great architect Maya had shown the demons, pouring a storm of weapons — arrows, spears, blazing darts — on Pradyumna, who as a great bowman endured it, the science answering every shaft.
statements.evidence: BP 10.55.20-21: 'sa ca māyāṃ samāśritya daiteyīṃ maya-darśitam / bādhyamāno 'stra-varṣeṇa raukmiṇeyo mahā-rathaḥ'. The vidya countering the shafts is the story's application of the Maha-vidya's stated power.

statements.claim: The demon cast his last illusion — a hundred conjured forms, yakshas and gandharvas, pishachas and serpents and rakshasis — but Pradyumna's Maha-vidya saw them for empty tricks of Maya and they dissolved one by one.
statements.evidence: BP 10.55.22: 'tato gauhyaka-gāndharva-paiśācoraga-rākṣasīḥ'; pack rendered excerpt: 'countered his hundred forms of maya'.

statements.claim: Pradyumna raised his sharpened sword and cut off Shambara's head — crown and earrings and all — and the illusions vanished with their master.
statements.evidence: BP 10.55.23: 'niśātam asim udyamya sa-kirīṭaṃ sa-kuṇḍalam' (raising the sharpened sword, [cutting off the head] with its crown and earrings); pack excerpt: 'with his sharp sword cut off the demon's head'.

statements.claim: With the deed done, Pradyumna turned toward the city of his father, Dvaraka, where his mother was still waiting.
statements.evidence: VP 5.27 (in pack): 'he proceeded to his father's house, where he alighted, along with Máyávatí, in the inner apartments'; closing lines are connective continuity into the next story.

notes: Story's tradition_note on the VP's numbered illusions (seven foiled, eighth mastered and turned back) matches the pack's VP excerpt verbatim. The framed beheading (crown and earrings) is the pack reading, not an invention.

statements.claim: Pradyumna descended from the sky into the inner palace of Dvaraka, escorted and showered with flowers by praising celestials, landing in the inner quarters with a woman (Mayavati) at his side.
statements.evidence: BP 10.55.24-25: 'ākīryamāṇo divi-jaiḥ stuvadbhiḥ kusumotkaraiḥ / antaḥ-pura-varaṃ...'; Harivamsha 1.255: 'descended from the sky with Māyāvati at the inner appartment of Keshava'.

statements.claim: He was dark as a rain cloud, wrapped in yellow silk, his face like a lotus, dark curls at his temples; the women of the palace found his resemblance to their lord uncanny.
statements.evidence: BP 10.55.26-28: 'jalada-śyāmaṃ pīta-kauśeya-vāsasam / sv-alaṅkṛta-mukhāmbhojaṃ nīla-vakrālakālibhiḥ'; the resemblance motif is Rukmini's own later reflection (v32, sārūpya with the bearer of Sharnga).

statements.claim: Rukmini looked at him long and wondered who this jewel among men was, whose lotus-eyed son he could be, how he had come to resemble the bearer of the Sharnga bow so exactly — whether he was the child she had carried.
statements.evidence: BP 10.55.29-33: 'ko nv ayam nara-vaidūryaḥ kasya vā kamalekṣaṇaḥ / mama cāpy ātmajo naṣṭo nīto yaḥ sūtikā-gṛhāt / kathaṃ tv anena samprāptaṃ sārūpyaṃ śārṅga-dhanvanaḥ / sa eva vā bhaven nūnaṃ yo me garbhe dhṛto 'rbhakaḥ'.

statements.claim: She spoke aloud, half to herself: blessed is the woman whose son is such a beautiful boy — resembling Kama himself, just entering the first stage of youth; had death not carried her baby away, her Pradyumna would have been of this age by now.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.255 (in pack): 'Blessed is that woman whose son is such a beautiful, long-lived boy resembling Kāma and just ushered into the first stage of youth... if the powerful Death had not carried him away my baby Pradyumna would have been of this age by this time.'

statements.claim: The marks of the Vrishni line were on him; his face and hair were the face and hair of Narayana.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.255 (in pack): 'you are a prince of the Vrishni family; from the marks of your body you look like Janārddana without his discus. Your face and hairs resemble those of Nārāyana.'

statements.claim: Krishna, who knew everything, said nothing and let the moment ripen.
statements.evidence: BP 10.55.34-35: 'evaṃ mīmāṃsamaṇāyāṃ vaidarbhyāṃ devakī-sutaḥ / vijñātārtho 'pi bhagavāṃs tūṣṇīm āsa janārdanaḥ'.

statements.claim: Narada came and told the whole story — the theft from the lying-in room, the casting into the sea, the fish, the demon's kitchen, the woman who raised the boy, the slaying of Shambara — and the palace filled with wonder and joy.
statements.evidence: Pack rendered excerpt (BP 10.55.24-39): 'when Narada told the whole tale, Rukmini, Devaki and Vasudeva embraced the couple in joy'; Harivamsha 1.255 has Krishna entering 'hearing from Nārada of the destruction of Shamvara'. 'As he so often did when a tale needed telling' is connective color.

statements.claim: Then Devaki and Vasudeva came, and Krishna and Balarama, and the palace women; Pradyumna saluted his mother and Govinda and bowed to Balarama; Krishna raised his eldest son, embraced him and smelt his head.
statements.evidence: BP 10.55.37: 'devakī vasudevaś ca kṛṣṇa-rāmau tathā striyaḥ'; Harivamsha 1.255: 'Having saluted his mother and Govinda Pradyumna bowed unto Haladhara. Thereupon raising up Pradyumna... Keshava... embraced him and smelt his head.'

statements.claim: Krishna presented the young woman to Rukmini as Rati, beloved of Kama, wife of her son and their eldest daughter-in-law in all but name, who had raised him and brought him home; Rukmini raised her daughter-in-law, set her on her lap and embraced her.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.255 (in pack): Krishna: 'Know her as Rati, the beloved consort of Kāma... this auspicious and chaste lady is the wife of your son... She is our eldest daughter-in-law and deserves our affection'; 'Rukshmini... raised up her daughter-in-law adorned with gold, placed her on her lap and embraced her.'

statements.claim: Dvaraka celebrated Pradyumna as one returned from the dead, and Rukmini led her son and daughter-in-law by the hand to her own rooms.
statements.evidence: BP 10.55.38: 'naṣṭaṃ pradyumnam āyātam ākarṇya dvārakaukasaḥ' with pack excerpt ('Dvaraka celebrated him as one returned from the dead'); Harivamsha 1.255: 'Rukshmini took her son who had returned with his wife to her own room'.

notes: Rukmini mourning 'like an osprey over an empty nest' restates the kurarī simile of BP 10.55.14 from the preceding event — consistent corpus continuity.

statements.claim: Rukmi of Bhojakata gave his granddaughter Rocana (his son's daughter) in marriage to Aniruddha, Krishna's grandson (Rukmi's own daughter's son).
statements.evidence: BP 10.61.24: 'dauhitrāyāniruddhāya pautrīṃ rukmy ādadād dhareḥ' (Rukmi gave his son's daughter to Aniruddha, Hari's daughter's son); pack excerpt names Rocana; VP 5.28: 'he betrothed the maiden (who was his son's daughter) to the son of his own daughter (her cousin Aniruddha)'.

statements.claim: Rukmi still nursed enmity against Krishna over an old humiliation.
statements.evidence: BP 10.61.22: 'yady apy anusmaran vairaṃ rukmī kṛṣṇāvamānitaḥ' (though Rukmi, humiliated by Krishna, remembered his enmity). The 'grudge nursed for years / old humiliation' framing is the pack's own rendering of this verse.

statements.claim: Setting his grudge aside for his sister Rukmini's sake, Rukmi agreed to the match; Krishna had asked for Rocana's hand for Aniruddha.
statements.evidence: Pack rendered excerpt (BP 10.61.19-26): 'Though he still nursed enmity against Krishna, Rukmi, to please his sister Rukmini, gave his granddaughter Rocana in marriage to Aniruddha'; VP 5.28: 'Keśava demanded in marriage for him the granddaughter of Rukmin'.

statements.claim: Aniruddha was the son of Pradyumna, whom Rukmi's daughter had chosen at her swayamvara years before; he was known as powerful and gallant, fierce in fight, the tamer of his foes.
statements.evidence: VP 5.28 (in pack): 'The heroic Pradyumna was chosen for her lord, at her public choice of a husband, by the daughter of Rukmin; and he had by her the powerful and gallant prince Aniruddha, who was fierce in fight, an ocean of prowess, and the tamer of his foes.'

statements.claim: Rukmini, Balarama, Krishna and a train of Yadavas journeyed to Bhojakata for the wedding, and the city made ready with garlands and celebration.
statements.evidence: BP 10.61.25: 'tasminn abhyudaye rājan rukmiṇī rāma-keśavau' (at that festival Rukmini, Rama and Kesava [went]); VP 5.28: 'Ráma and other Yádavas attended Krishńa to Bhojakat́a, the city of Rukmin.' Decorations/gifts are generic wedding color.

statements.claim: Aniruddha and Rocana were cousins through both lines of Rukmi's blood — the daughter's son and the son's daughter — and the wedding joined the divided families.
statements.evidence: VP 5.28 (in pack): Rocana is Rukmi's 'son's daughter', Aniruddha 'the son of his own daughter'; both lines descend from Rukmi. The reconciliation-at-the-wedding reading matches BP's 'to please his sister Rukmini'.

statements.claim: The Yadavas rode the road that Rukmi had once sworn no one from Dvaraka would travel again.
statements.evidence: No source records any such oath; it is rhetorical heightening of the well-supported long feud and humiliation (BP 10.61.22), not an asserted, checkable event — treated as scene-setting rather than a sourceable fact.

statements.claim: When the celebrations ended the party from Dvaraka rode home, the two families were one again, and the wedding at Bhojakata would be remembered as the day the quarrel ended.
statements.evidence: The pack's own VP 5.28 passage shows the celebration ending otherwise: right after the wedding, Kalinga and other kings incited Rukmi to a dice game with Balarama ('he engaged Balaráma at a game of dice in the palace... Halayudha, galled by the broad laughter of the Kalinga prince, and the contemptuous speech of Rukmin, was exceedingly angry'), and the VP chapter header in the pack states: 'Balaráma beat at dice, becomes incensed, and slays Rukmin and others.' The feud thus did not end at this wedding — it ended in Rukmi's death during it.

corrections.original_sentence: When the celebrations ended and the party from Dvaraka rode home, the two families were one again — joined at last by the very thing that had once divided them, and the wedding at Bhojakata would be remembered afterward as the day the quarrel ended.
corrections.suggested: But the old quarrel had not run its course: before the celebrations were over, Kalinga and other kings goaded Rukmi into a dice game with Balarama, and when Rukmi's taunts roused the enraged Balarama the wedding ended in blood, with Rukmi slain — remembered not as the day the quarrel ended but as the day it claimed him.

notes: The story stops before the dice episode (its cited BP range 10.61.19-26 ends just before it), but the pack itself carries the VP account of the dice quarrel and its header ('Balaráma beat at dice, becomes incensed, and slays Rukmin and others'), so the closing claim of a peaceful, permanent reconciliation at this very wedding contradicts the pack.

statements.claim: Bana, son of Bali, always devoted to Shiva, ruled over the pleasant city of Shonitapura and had a thousand arms given him by the god.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.2-3, 7: 'tasyaurasaḥ suto bānaḥ śiva-bhakti-rataḥ sadā / śoṇitākhye pure ramye sa rājyam akarot purā'; 'doḥ-sahasraṃ tvayā dattaṃ'.

statements.claim: Bana had begun to find his thousand arms a burden — there were only so many weapons a man could hold — and his pride had grown until he believed no enemy was worthy of him.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.7: 'doḥ-sahasraṃ tvayā dattaṃ paraṃ bhārāya me 'bhavat' (the thousand arms you gave have become a great burden to me). The psychologizing of his pride is connective narration consistent with v5 'vīrya-durmadaḥ' (mad with pride of valor) and v9-10 (Shiva angry, Bana delighted).

statements.claim: Bana stood before Shiva and addressed him: 'I bow to you, Mahadeva, teacher and lord of the worlds. The thousand arms you gave me have become a burden; they itch for battle, and I wish to test them against the great elephants that guard the quarters of the world.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.6-8: 'namasye tvāṃ mahā-deva lokānāṃ gurum īśvaram / doḥ-sahasraṃ tvayā dattaṃ paraṃ bhārāya me 'bhavat / kaṇḍūtyā nibhṛtair dorbhir yuyutsur dig-gajān aham'.

statements.claim: Shiva grew angry at the pride of his worshipper and declared: 'When your banner falls, then your pride will be humbled, in battle with a rival worthy of you.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.9: 'tac chrutvā bhagavān kruddhaḥ ketus te bhajyate yadā'; pack rendered excerpt: 'Shiva declared that when Bana's flag fell, his pride would be humbled in battle with a peer.'

statements.claim: Bana heard a promise in the warning and went home delighted, imagining the battle to come and never wondering what kind of battle would humble his pride.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.10: 'ity uktaḥ kumatir hṛṣṭaḥ sva-gṛhaṃ prāviśan nṛpa' (thus addressed, the foolish one, delighted, entered his house). The final image of the banner over the gates is connective scene-setting.

notes: 'Eldest son of Bali' follows the pack's index entry and excerpt. Shiva as 'the refuge of his devotees, kind to those who love him' renders BP 10.62.4 ('śaraṇyo bhakta-vatsalaḥ').

statements.claim: Usha, daughter of Bana, king of Shonitapura, woke calling for a man she had never seen — 'where are you, my beloved?' — after dreaming of a dark, lotus-eyed youth.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.11-12, 15: 'tasyoṣā nāma duhitā svapne prādyumninā ratim... kvāsi kānteti vādinī'; 'dṛṣṭaḥ kaścin naraḥ svapne śyāmaḥ kamala-locanaḥ'.

statements.claim: The dream had been promised her: having seen Parvati sporting with Shiva, Usha wished for such a husband, and the goddess told her that he who appeared to her in a dream on the twelfth night of the bright fortnight of Vaishakha would be her lord.
statements.evidence: VP 5.32 (in pack): 'Ushá, the daughter of Báńa, having seen Párvatí sporting with her lord, Śambhu, was inspired with a wish for similar dalliance. The beautiful Gaurí... said... He who shall appear to you, princess, in a dream on the twelfth lunation of the light half of Vaiśákha, he will be your husband.'

statements.claim: Her friend Chitralekha, daughter of Bana's minister Kumbhanda — skilled in painting and a yogini — found her pining and asked: 'Whom do you seek, fair-browed one? What is the desire in your heart?'
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.13-14, 21: 'bāṇasya mantrī kumbhāṇḍaś citralekhā ca tat-sutā / kaṃ tvaṃ mṛgayase su-bhru kīdṛśas te manorathaḥ'; 'citralekhā... yoginī'.

statements.claim: Usha answered that she sought a man seen in a dream, dark, with lotus-petal eyes, whose lips she longed to taste — but she could not name him or his home.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.16: 'tam ahaṃ mṛgaye kāntaṃ pāyayitvādharaṃ madhu' (I seek him as my lover, having drunk the honey of his lips). The inability to name him follows from the dream (v11-12).

statements.claim: Chitralekha painted the gods, gandharvas, siddhas, charanas and the serpents of the deep, and then, among the great houses of men, the Vrishnis — and the face of Krishna himself, and after it his grandson Aniruddha, son of Pradyumna.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.18-20: 'ity uktvā deva-gandharva siddha-cāraṇa-pannagān / manujeṣu ca sā vṛṣṇīn śūram ānakadundubhim / aniruddhaṃ vilikhitaṃ...'. The verse names the Vrishnis and the hero Anakadundubhi (Vasudeva) before Aniruddha; listing Krishna's face among the Vrishni portraits is a natural connective rendering of 'the Vrishnis' (he is the line's foremost figure), and Usha's recognition falls on Aniruddha as in the source.

statements.claim: Seeing Aniruddha's portrait Usha cried 'This is he! This is he!' and then dropped her gaze, her cheeks burning with shame at her secret; Chitralekha, the yogini, recognized the youth as Krishna's grandson.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.20-21: 'aniruddhaṃ vilikhitaṃ vīkṣyoṣāvāṅ-mukhī hriyā / citralekhā tam ājñāya pautraṃ kṛṣṇasya yoginī' (seeing painted Aniruddha, Usha lowered her face in shame; the yogini Chitralekha knew him as Krishna's grandson); VP 5.32: 'This is he! this is he!'

statements.claim: Dvaraka was a city so far from Shonitapura that it might have been another world, with no road leading from Usha's chambers to it.
statements.evidence: The distance and impossibility are the story's framing of the abduction to come (next story, BP 10.62.21-25); no source quantifies the distance. Not asserted as a checkable fact.

notes: Story follows the BP opening (dream first) while weaving in the VP's Parvati-promise frame, exactly as its tradition_note says the sources relate — both frames are present in the pack.

statements.claim: Chitralekha set out from Shonitapura, crossed the distance to Dvaraka, and by her yogic power found Aniruddha (Pradyumna's son) asleep on a beautiful couch in his inner chamber and carried the sleeping prince back to Shonitapura.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.21-22: 'citralekhā tam ājñāya pautraṃ kṛṣṇasya yoginī / tatra suptaṃ su-paryaṅke prādyumniṃ yogam āsthitā' (knowing him, the yogini, employing her power, [brought] Pradyumna's son who slept on a fine couch). The one-night crossing and 'he did not wake' are connective elaboration of the yogic transport; the pack's own excerpt says she 'flew to Dvaraka'.

statements.claim: Usha, overjoyed at seeing the youth of her dream, dressed him in the finest garments, wound garlands about him, set scents, incense and lamps burning about him, and placed him in the seat of honor in her chambers.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.23-24: 'sā ca taṃ sundara-varaṃ vilokya muditānanā / parārdhya-vāsaḥ-srag-gandha-dhūpa-dīpāsanādibhiḥ' (beholding the handsome youth, her face joyful, [she honored him] with supremely valuable garments, garlands, fragrance, incense, lamps and seats).

statements.claim: Aniruddha came to live hidden in the innermost women's quarters of Bana's palace, and day after day passed with no one perceiving it, while Usha's love grew.
statements.evidence: BP 10.62.25: 'gūḍhaḥ kanyā-pure śaśvat-pravṛddha-snehayā tayā' (hidden in the maidens' quarters, with her love ever increasing).

statements.claim: The guards at every outer gate made the inner chambers where no man was permitted the safest walls in the city.
statements.evidence: Why the secret held is not detailed in BP 10.62.21-25 beyond 'hidden in the maidens' quarters'; the guarded-women's-quarters logic is connective framing consistent with the verse.

statements.claim: But eyes in the palace were beginning to notice the strangeness, and the days of the hidden love were numbered.
statements.evidence: Foreshadowing of the next corpus event (Bana captures and binds Aniruddha, per pack corpus chain and BP 10.62.26ff), phrased as narrative tease, not an asserted sourceable fact.

notes: The story follows the BP version (sleeping prince carried by yogic power) and flags the Harivamsha variant (awake, Gandharva marriage) in its tradition_note — both present in the pack (BP passage + Harivamsha 1.266 excerpt).
